review:
[b]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/b] hit a home run and is a more than worthy sequel to the already fantastic [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/ready2b/recommended/387290]Ori and the Blind Forest[/url]. This sublime experience combines the best of storytelling with delightful action-platforming to create my [b]favorite gaming experience of 2020.[/b]

[u][b]Played with PlayStation 4 controller[/b][/u]

[h1]✔️[u]Positive:[/u][/h1]
[b][+] Versatile movement in a beautiful metroidvania.[/b] 
As you progress and obtain more abilities (even more than the first game), Ori gradually becomes more monkey-like in their movements, opening up the world for more exploration.  The whole map essentially becomes a delightful playground with hidden nuggets/collectibles in every nook and cranny. Thanks to the responsive controls, the different mechanics can easily be combined with one another to result in fast, agile, and fluid movement - which happens to be the perfect accompaniment for the exciting escape sequences and the thrilling boss fights.

[b][+] Emotional and thrilling storytelling.[/b] 
The incredible writing and direction, supported by the beautiful art and the divine OST makes the whole experience feel like a fairytale brought to life. I wouldn’t dare to deprive you from such a wonderful story by spoiling it here, so do yourself a favor and get the game. I will openly admit that I cried like a baby multiple times.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2169324939
[b][+] This sequel makes several notable improvements compared to the first game:[/b]
[olist]
[*][b]Auto-save.[/b]
Thank God they removed the manual save system introduced in the first game.

[*][b]New combat system![/b] 
Ori no longer has only the auto-lock on spirit fire attack, which I personally didn’t care for. Instead you can unlock and upgrade multiple abilities (including melee and ranged attacks), which can be assigned to the X, Y, B (Square, Triangle and Circle for PlayStation) buttons at your leisure. Combat options were lacking in the original so really appreciate this customization upgrade. Personally, I couldn’t get enough of the giant hammer and Shock Smash upgrade. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2177313275
[*][b]Addition of equipables![/b] 
Similar to the charms in Hollow Knight, Ori can now equip Spirit Shards (equippable items that provide upgrades to you or your abilities). Again, I find that the customization options allow for a more self-tailored experience. I basically had two sets of Spirit Shards that suited my playstyle: one for exploration and one for combat.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2177313407
[*][b]Improvements to the map and teleportation.[/b] 
The map immediately displays any warpstone and collectable you come across without requiring a map upgrade first (as was the case in the original). The map also makes it abundantly clear where the objective is, which areas you have and haven’t explored yet, and it even shows your latest movement in the form of a dotted line, making it incredibly difficult to get lost or disoriented. Furthermore, you can now teleport to any warpstone from any location, which greatly reduces the necessity for backtracking and helps to keep the pace of the game up. 

[*][b]Addition of side quests is always a blessing.[/b] 
Several great side quests were included in this title but there was one in particular that I really enjoyed: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2177313569]“hand to hand”.[/url] It is essentially a trade sequence quest where you aid the next NPC by providing them with the item the previous NPC gave you. Helping the many creatures felt like I was contributing to the livelihood of the forest.

[*][b]Addition of a main hub.[/b] 
Important NPCs, such as vendors, relocate to the main hub in Wellspring Glades, after you meet them in the wild. Since the land is plagued by corruption and is tyrannized by the evil Shriek, NPCs will immigrate to this safe haven, inadvertently creating a diverse community. By offering resources, such as Gorlek ore and mysterious seeds, found during your journey to Grom (builder) and Tuley (gardener), you are also able to upgrade the main hub until it turns into a lively village. Investing in the community felt rewarding, and encouraged me to search for all the collectable items and help all NPCs.
[/olist]

[b][+] The game provides the necessary tools to unlock everything without relying on external help/guides.[/b]
If collecting everything is your cup of tea (it certainly is mine), then you will probably appreciate this point. There are map upgrades you can either buy or obtain which mark the location of all missing collectables, making them much easier to obtain. Furthermore, if you need to farm for more currency, Spirit Shards can be used to speed up the process; for example, by combining Consume (Enemies have 70% more Life and deal 70% more damage, but drop double currency) with Turmoil (Enemies respawn faster).

[b][+] Perhaps a minor detail but the game automatically pauses if your controller disconnects[/b]. 
Kudos, Moon Studios.

[h1]➖[u]Neutral:[/u][/h1]
[b][-] I enjoyed playing it so much that finishing it felt bitter-sweet.[/b]
As much as I loved the game, I felt sad knowing that it would be a while before another game would blow me away like this again. I’m sure most of us have at least one game that we wish we would wipe from our memories and replay again - Ori and the Will of the Wisps falls under this category. [u]Can’t wait for the next installment![/u]

[h1]🏅[u]Verdict:[/u][/h1]
[h1]★★★★★ Marvellous[/h1]
A practically-flawless sequel and a must-have if you enjoyed Ori and the Blind Forest. Highly recommended to everyone else.

For anyone who didn't play the predecessor Ori and the Blind Forest, I highly recommend playing that one first! It's cheaper, it's shorter, it has fewer abilities to get used to, and it's generally less difficult. If you like the first Ori, you'll probably like the second one too (I did)! 

For anyone who played Ori and the Blind Forest, you'll probably love this one too! But just in case, here is what changed / was expanded upon:
- It's roughly twice as long (100% completion on hard without hardcore achievements like one life)
- It has all the original movement abilities and multiple new ones, which lets you zip through the air more than ever before. :) And that becomes necessary too in many sections
- There is much higher focus on different combat abilities: Fast melee, heavy melee, fast ranged, heavy ranged, and they're all viable to play too! This is the biggest change, so if you absolutely dislike platformer combat, check out some gameplay videos first. No, it's not as difficult as Hollow Knight!
- Another big change: no more manual saving (!) That really took getting used to, but the autosaves are very frequent, so you never lose considerable progress, no worries. Also, there are multiple autosaves, so you shouldn't be able to softlock your save.
- There are escape sequences again, one of which is far more difficult than any in Blind Forest but has been supposedly toned down a bit since a day before writing this review
- There are now bossfights alongside the escape sequences (but they're not awful, you don't get oneshot or anything)
- Spirit light is now a currency and you can use it to buy upgrades (basically like before), get new combat abilities, and upgrade your upgrades+abilities. No, you will never get stuck if you skip everything, the progress-required abilities are all free
- There are now collectibles which you can equip to give you some passive effects (risk-reward combat effects, upgrades to your ranged abilities, movement abilities etc.)
- There are also collectibles to make your haven prettier, the place where you can buy stuff 
- There are multiple optional quests which reward you with equippable upgrades or spirit light to buy stuff
- There is a way to see all secrets on the map by the near end of the game, which is great for anyone who wants to 100% without an external map (like me)

Highly recommended, one of my favorite platformers :)

It’s been over a month since I finished Ori and the Will of the Wisps, and it’s safe to say it quickly became one of my all time favourite games I’ve ever played. This sequel is a complete step up from the first. The concerns I had from the first game were vastly improved in this continuation of the story. 

Ori and the Will of the Wisps follows a spirit named Ori who must rescue an owl named Ku and heal the decaying world around them. After a foe separates them, Ori must navigate the new lands to find Ku. Along the journey, you’ll be introduced to new biomes, characters and improved combat mechanics. 

What I liked about this game was how gorgeous it is. There’s no doubt that the creators put their blood, sweat and tears into making it so visually vibrant and detailed. I have over 500 screenshots of this game and each area never failed to leave me in awe. 

The gameplay, from the combat to platforming, was very well executed and linear. If you’re familiar with the Blind Forest, various areas of the map require certain abilities to unlock. With that said, there will be lots of exploring and backtracking to get those abilities. The exploration of your home base was a nice touch as well. Having these little quests in between exploring was a fun time figuring out what goes to whom and solving the puzzles. I appreciated the spirit shrines and spirit trials. Those were a nice addition to improve your time and speed. They were quite challenging and I think it’s a great way to get better at that aspect of the game if you truly wanted to get 100% achievements. The chase sequences, if you read my previous review for the Blind Forest, you already know I HATED that part of the game and I still do lol. However, this time around it seemed to be less difficult? Certainly less frustrating and punishing than the Blind Forest. 

The storyline… guys, this storyline was just so damn good. I thought the first game was emotional, wrong, this one made me cry like a baby. Just when you thought things were alright, the devs decided to punch you in the gut with the fate of some of the characters. I won’t say more because I want this review to be spoiler free in terms of the events in the game. 

In the near future, I for sure see myself coming back to this game to spend time on my platforming skills and get the 100% achievement. Overall, Ori and the Will of the Wisps is definitely a game worth sinking all your time into and your money's worth.

I don't know if Moon Studio will release a sequel, but I'm sure the Ori series is a masterpiece you'll never regret.

I very rarely use the word 'perfection' when describing my opinion on a game.
But this is 1000% deserving of that word. It feels like the PEAK of game design.

Visuals are outrageously gorgeous.
Soundtrack is heavenly.
Characters are awesome, memorable and unique in the best way.
Story was surprisingly emotional. 

I expected it to have a predictable ending, and yet it still threw a curveball and got me misty-eyed.

The first game was amazing too, but this... this is art. 
God, this franchise is just a must-play for everyone.

Short Version: Whether on sale or not, this game is totally worth it. If you liked Blind Forest, this will continue that love. Honestly, I have to give Will of the Wisps a 10 out of 10. Right now at the time of writing, this is on sale for $10??? BUY IT. 

Long Version: There's so much to love about Ori and the Will of the Wisps. Let's dive into it. 

Mechanics: The powers you get this time around, are fresh and interesting. They make sense, though you may struggle for a bit to get a hang of some of the powers in the beginning. 

Story: Seriously, just a kick in the feels, right from the start. In our last game, Ori got a family. In this game... well, Ori's family goes through some hard times, including some serious loss. The characters experience pain and loss differently, and not just once, but several times. However, this really does wrap up Ori's story very well. I really enjoyed, though I was struggling from time to time, this story. Though I was sad for the one who shunned the light. 

New Characters: There are some great new characters in Ori, and some of our old faves. Some of these characters are really well done. Some are just functional, but I really liked some of the bosses and their stories. Not everyone has a happy end. 

Controls: Precise and Intuitive. Ori does what you want, when you want. No issues here. 

Combat: It's Ori! Combat is seriously fun and well thought out. There are some annoying features when it comes to some enemies, but even on my last play through for a speed run, I figured out some new tricks to make them easier. Experiment, experiment, experiment. 

Music & Voice Acting: Ori has brilliant music that seems to match each and every scene perfectly. Fast paced beats with heavy dark tones when you're running for your life to mellow sad notes, that seem to tug at your heart... Whomever composed this really did a great job. The voice cast is small, this isn't a dialogue game, however, there is effort and it fits and is done well.

Graphics: Honestly, I didn't really expect much going into Ori. I mean, we're talking about a side-scrolling metroidvania with our lovable Black and White Hero, Ori. But, boy was I wrong. There is loving detail put into each and every area. The added effects everywhere in the game, will just blow you away. For extra oomph, go into settings and just run everything up to max. Seriously, why would we need max in a game like this? It allows the game to bring the background and extra effects to life. It's pretty amazing. It's no wonder the game won for Outstanding Visual Style. 

Achievements: I've got 35 out of 37 and I'm done and lazy at this point. Perhaps I'll go back and get the last two, but just needing a different game at the moment. Most of the achievements are fun and help you enjoy a second play through. Some are annoying in that they push you to be perfect, but some people love that. 

Save System: Well that's weird, there are auto-backups which you can access if you need to, so that's helpful and annoying if you're trying to do a flawless run. Knowing which save is actually the save you want can sometimes be hard to tell. 

Overall: This game is really amazing. I got it on sale but I would have paid full price had I known what I was getting. It's come out to just around $1/hour and each and every hour were jam packed with entertainment.... Except maybe the speed trials. Seriously though, if you liked Blind Forest, you're probably going to love this. I don't know why some people thought this was worse than Blind Forest. Makes no sense. Though it does put a cap on the story. I spent hours exploring beautiful landscapes brought to life by gorgeous backgrounds and awesome music, all while helping Ori and the Wisps.

Ori and the Will of the Wisps, from a pure video game experience, is my favorite video game of all time. Gameplay is magnificent, the visuals are stunning, the story is emotional and heartfelt; it literally has it all! In my opinion, it is the most complete gameplay experience that I've ever had. 

This all may sound hyperbolic to most people, and I'll admit, these claims are very extreme. But I would not state my opinions this way if I didn't believe them. Let me break down the reasons why I love this game so much a bit further. I will note that this review is mostly spoiler free, so if you want to experience the game yourself--which I obviously highly recommend--you should still be able to read this review to get a good picture for what you would be getting into. 

Gameplay Design: The gameplay is that of any typical 2D metroidvania title. You explore a large world and come across upgrades and discover secrets along the way to make traversal easier throughout the game. It also encourages you to backtrack to old areas by sprinkling in hints of knowledge of where certain items are so you can return later with the appropriate upgrade. This also allows more skilled players a chance to test their skills and try and get certain items faster if they are creative enough with their current repertoire. The way you upgrade Ori is also wildly fun and flexible. In a respectful nod to the medtroidvania juggernaut "Hollow Knight," "Ori and the Will of the Wisps" adopts a similar upgrade system to the "charms" in Hollow Knight with the "shard" system. Hidden throughout the map are different shards you can equip to made your gameplay experience more dynamic, and you can equip or unequip shards at any time you want. It is a system that is extremely fun to play with to fit whatever situation you find yourself in, and the shards are fun to find too!

Combat System: One of the major criticisms of this games predecessor, "Ori and the Blind Forest," was that the combat was very limited, and that there were no boss fights. This aspect of the game has been markedly improved. There are a variety of combat options for Ori to choose from in this game, and they all have their own unique advantages and disadvantages in certain situations. You can choose up to three at a time to have on your face buttons, and this gives combat a much larger part of the experience this time around. Plus, the game also has multiple dynamic boss fights that will put your skills to the test! 

Platforming: On the other hand, one of the aspects of gameplay that the predecessor was most famous for was the platforming sections, as well as some unique movement abilities. I am pleased to say that this game has all of these elements as well! The platforming is probably even better than in its predecessor, with more variety of ways to move Ori around throughout the map. Needless to say, it is even more fun to move around as Ori in this game.

Map Design: The game flows seamlessly, and the reason that is the case is because of the masterful map design. The way the map is laid out makes going from one area to the next intuitive. Sometimes the game feels linear, only for you to realize that its just because the map is designed in a way that gently pushes you in a specific direction using visual cues. Its actually quite clever. The areas all fit together in a way that makes sense, and this game actually does something that is very difficult; it fits a wide range of different environments in relative proximity to each other with it actually making sense in the world!

Story: No story spoilers here, but just know that the if you played the first Ori game, that the story will probably move you just as much, if not even more than that game. It is definitely something that should be experiences at least once. 

Art Direction: The Ori series has always been well known for its gorgeous visuals. This game uses a combination of hand painted backgrounds with 3D character models that works immaculately. The game is masterful at using both the foreground and background to its advantage, with both characters and enemies jumping out of the foreground into the playable plane, which makes the game more immersive. The animations for the characters are fluid, with Ori in particular being a joy to watch; the way he jumps, the way he runs, the way he climbs, all the say down to the small details like Ori doing a handstand on top of a pole. This all makes the game that much more endearing to experience.

Sound: I will say this right now; this OST is my favorite of any video game I've played. I have a moderate music background, so I'm particular about my music. This OST makes fantastic uses of leitmotifs to let you musically understand what's going on in the game at that moment. At the same time, it uses a vareity of melody modulation and mode mixture to give a bit of spice to certain tracks. Not to mention that every area does have a unique sound of its own, and every cinematic moment in the story is enhanced by the OST to an insane degree. The sound design is also superb, with certain actions feeling extremely powerful and satisfying. There are also the little details like the little grunts Ori makes while swinging weapons, to gasps when he emerges from water.  

Technical Performance: Heavy criticism was given to this game upon launch for its many technical hiccups, and rightfully so. People have complained of stuttering, screen tearing, frame rate drops glitches where characters disappear, music glitches, to not even saving achievements. That being said, I want to emphasize that if that is your main reason for not getting this game, that these issues are (for the most part) resolved. There have been multiple patches to the game, and the developers have ironed out ALL of these issues. In my experience playing the game, I haven't experienced a SINGLE ONE of these issues. The game flowed seamlessly, no stuttering, minimal load times, and runs at a butter smooth FPS (mine was not capped so ran at 200+ FPS), all in 4K resolution. As far as technical performance, this game really doesn't have any issues, at least with my experience.  

Conclusions: Overall, this game as a lot of love put into it. You can tell the developers took their time with this game and came out with the best product that they could produce! This game is an absolute masterpiece, and is the new gold standard in which future metroidvania titles should be compared to.

[code]Ori and the Will of the Wisps is an excellent Metroidvania-style game that’s simply a must-play for every fan of the genre. However, make no mistake – despite its appearance, the game can be quite challenging[/code]

Released in 2015, [url]Ori and the Blind Forest[/url] was a surprise hit, since it was the first-ever game from developer Moon Studios. It received impressive reviews ([url=https://opencritic.com/game/829/ori-and-the-blind-forest]OpenCritic score: 90[/url]) with a lot of praise in regards to its story, visuals, gameplay and music, although some other aspects of the game – mostly the combat, short game length with little replay value and some occasional frustrations thanks to difficulty spikes - [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ori_and_the_Blind_Forest#Reception]were met with criticism[/url]. Despite last playing it in 2018, I still remember how frustrating some of the escape sequences could be in particular.

Five years after the initial game, in 2020, [i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] released, a sequel that’s not only continuing the story but also aims to address the aforementioned criticisms. The combat has been reworked, as you’re no longer spamming Sein’s flames – instead, one of the first skills that can be obtained for Ori is the “Spirit Edge”, a sword of light for melee combat. In fact, there are multiple new active skills to be found which provide new options to attack enemies – for example, Ori can now use a bow (“Spirit Arc”) which makes for a great (ranged) combat option. The same can’t be said for all of the new abilities, unfortunately, as I found some of them to be quite a lot weaker than others. Still, overall I found the combat to be much improved, although I’d still argue that it’s probably the weakest aspects of the game. It’s fine but since you’ll mostly fight the same standard enemies over and over again, it can get quite repetitive. And considering just how good the remaining game is, just being “fine” simply sticks out.

To no surprise, [i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] looks and sounds exceptionally well, just like the first game did. I didn’t encounter any performance or technical problems and was pleased to see that the game supports HDR as well, although I wish the game provided better options to set it up right (e.g., example pictures). The music, once again composed by Gareth Coker, [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sE6JXUghfgk]is a delight[/url] and the visuals are a treat – I wouldn’t mind playing through 10+ games in the same art-style.

But what’s probably the best part about [i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] for me is traversing its world consisting out of multiple biomes. The most fun I had with the game was when I was figuring out the movement puzzles, especially the late-game ones that make use of all of Ori’s expanded movement skills. Gliding through the air, triple-jumping, dashing and then using the “Bash” ability to propel yourself forwards using hostile projectiles to cross that one gap - it’s these exhilarating moments that really made me love the game. Ori’s full movement set is full of different option to either gain height or cross vertical distances, but it never feels too complicated to use or even overloaded – I never had any trouble with the controls even with Ori’s full skill-set unlocked.

That said, while [i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] looks like an all-ages experience, it’s actually not without challenging moments, even on “normal” difficulty. The sequel took away with the ability to save at (almost) all times from [i]Ori and the Blind Forest[/i] and opted for auto-saves instead. While most of these auto-save-points are well placed, there are a few lengthy (jumping) puzzles – or the returning escape sequences - in the game that only offer a single checkpoint at the beginning, which can be quite frustrating if you only missed the last jump or something similar. Still, moments like these are an exception, with even some of the boss fights offering checkpoints in-between their various phases.

I found the boss fights of [i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] to be well-designed encounters with some nicely telegraphed moves, which ask you to make combine your combat and movement abilities in order to evade incoming attacks and strike at the right time. However, I do feel like the hitboxes of some of their attacks are hard to predict – especially since most of the bosses are quite big, with parts that hurt you, parts you need to hit to hurt them and parts that do nothing at all. Still, even with the occasional “why did that hit me?” moment, the boss fights never felt unfair – when I died, I always knew what went wrong on my end. If you want to ease the challenge, you could also always go for collecting all of the many life/mana upgrades for Ori in the game – this is a Metroidvania-style game after all.

What I adore about [i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] is that it’s a Metroidvania-style game that’s so well-designed that it manages to evade most of the problems of the genre. Thanks to various side quests and main quest icons on the map, for example, you’ll always know in which general direction to head next – but they’re never placed in a way that you lose out on the fun of discovering just how to get there, they’re just making sure you won’t look in an entirely wrong place of the big map. I also love the option to buy maps of the various places in the game, which show you a broad, grey outline of the rooms and corridors – making sure that you can’t miss entire rooms if you’re going for that 100% save. Additionally, you even got (pricier) options to buy map upgrades that show the location of various collectables.

[i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] also introduces a few timed races with online leaderboards, if you’re still not satisfied with 100%ing the game – although that admittedly doesn’t really increase the replayability of the game by much. There are achievements to beat the game without getting hit, without getting upgrades, in a short time and so on though, force those looking for excuses to play through it multiple times.

Thankfully, as long as you’re not going for the 100% save, you won’t spend too much time backtracking in the game, since the areas are smartly spread out and offer fast travel options to make sure you’ll get to new biomes quickly. After a straight progression during the first few hours, the game also opens up halfway through, allowing you to tackle the main story objectives in an order of your choosing. [i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] does an exceptional job of allowing you to discover new routes, areas and abilities while simultaneously providing just enough guidance so that you’ll never feel lost – an impressive feat.

Tying everything together is an emotional story told through few words but well-presented cutscenes instead which – in combination with the music - simply moved me to tears on a few occasions. I’ll admit that [i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] does not a tell an especially complex story, nor a very surprising one, but it’s told in such a heartfelt way that its emotional conclusion managed to keep me weeping throughout the entirety of the credits, which is as good as it gets.

Concluding, [i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] is an excellent Metroidvania-style game that - while not entirely without flaws – is certainly amongst the best games of the genre, improving on almost every aspect from it’s already great predecessor. It’s simply a must-play if you even remotely like the genre, although I recommend playing through the predecessor for story reasons first.

Ori and the Will of the Wisps once again proves that beautiful art direction and well-designed platforming blend together perfectly. It not only meets the high bar raised by its predecessor, it goes above and beyond everything you could have hoped for.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
If the first entry was a slow and precise blend of concise platforming mechanics, the sequel is a mesmerizing dance as you make your way from one area to the next using a plethora of new and unique techniques. At its essence, Ori and The Will of the Wisps is a pure metroidvania game. As you progress through the main story, new mechanics get introduced and your arsenal expands. The more agile Ori becomes, the more areas become available. The gameplay loop revolves around exploration, combat, platforming and puzzle-solving. The game borders on complexity without ever becoming complicated. Easy to learn but hard to master, the platforming requires quick reflexes, observational skills, precise button presses and a complete understanding of each mechanic. It is by no means an easy game, and if you expect to breeze through it without giving it the time it deserves, you will have a bad time. Even though I died a lot during my playthrough, it never felt unfair. I knew what I had done wrong and had only myself to blame. Thankfully, the game knows this and wastes no time sending you right back in. The movement feels smooth, level design is top-notch and has evolved and adapted to the game's new mechanics. The combat has also been massively expanded, with new attack moves, different abilities and distinctive traversal options. Quite simply, if you are a fan of platformers, this is a must-buy.

However, it is worth noting that some difficult enemy encounters are heavy ‘bullet sponges’, meaning it would take me almost half an hour of very repetitive combat to finally kill it. Although these encounters are very rare and are a minor nuisance in the grand scheme of things, it does take you out of an otherwise stellar experience.

Prepare for an anxiety-inducing orchestra of thunderous beats and unsettling melodies that will make your palms sweat. Are you taking in the scenery? Slow and heart-wrenching tunes play, making you smile and admire what videogames have become.

🍃 ORI AND THE WILL OF THE WISPS IS AN INDIE MASTERPIECE FINALE 🌳

REVIEWED ON: (GeForce GT 1030/i7-3770 )

-This review comes from a guy that has yet to re-play the first game and experience it to the end. Did try it back then, but never finished it.  However I can vouch for the sequel being a completely different and more amazing experience compared to it's predecessor. This said let's break it all into parts to make it easier, and you can all experience the journey on my channel as well if you'd like: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CquTuw_CeIQ&list=PLU-KGNqzKRtc&index=8

✨ PLOT: This is the story and conclussion of our protagonist Ori, whom eventually finds his reason to be born. A seedling of light brought to the world with a purpose and a legacy for centuries to come. He shall bring hope to his land, the world possibly, and erradicate the roots of evil that have plagued  his home for so long. The story has a message many would understand, but in order to do so you will need to beat it. Dramatic, sad, heart-breaking, and consequential moments await Ori, but all ends well when peace returns. Nothing shall be in vain, for the light is with him at all times.

✨ PERFORMANCE: The game worked surprisingly well for me, and there was no need to tune down the graphics much. I was able to experience the beauty of it's world, characters, music, and gameplay all in stable frames. This game is absolute cinema art in a canvas, playing with lag is not the way to go when we talk about how incredible it looks. This is one of the reasons I did not finish the first game back on my GTS450, and obviously the sequel would not launch for me until I got the GT1030. Some games are best taken seriously, not just to be played for fun. 

✨ RE-PLAYABILITY: OATWOTW has a single story which concludes everything, but as you progress in order to complete it all you will need to explore a lot, meet characters, learn the ropes of your skills, and unlock various zones to proceed and or get stronger with time. The game is beautiful, but also frustrating at times, when you're near the end you come to terms with the fact that you were possibly raging for nothing, it all becomes easy once you get certain skills you REALLY need to bypass obstacles. I play my games on easy/normal difficulty because I'm here for the story, but the hard settings may even be more frustrating than expect to many. After you beat the game, you will be able to return to your last save, and complete everything you might have missed before the grand finale. As a Metroidvania and platformer, the map is quite intense/vast and it will take you a while to explore every nook and cranny, and get everything along with the achievements. I, of course am not a completionist but many out there would love taking their time more than usual. There is no new game+ because the end is quite realistic, but you will have the freedom to teleport elsewhere from your last save location and 100% the game. 

✨ GAMEPLAY: The game has a lot to talk about, and is a perfect example of a great Metroidvania and GOTY in my opinion.  As you start playing as Ori, he is but a fragile light with the basic knowledge from the first game, with time you will discover a lot of skills to aid you on your quest, some a need, while others you can try for fun. This game is quite original with HP and Mana buffs. Your life and Mana bars are quite huge, it just requires exploring a lot and finding fragments to unite and become stronger. The game also has bonus quests by characters, some short and some long, and also some tough "racing" missions in a way. I skipped those, too much for me.  You will be free to adapt to your own playstyle by choosing the skills and weapons you really feel comfortable with, as I personally stuck up to the bow, flame, and sword up until reaching the end which requires a lot of precision and a special skill.  Once you are overpowered, bosses will fall fast, but of course I did play it on low difficulty so that might differ for you all. Remember to explore, talk to characters, meet vendors, and get stronger for a better less-infuriating experience. I did get stuck at times, but as far as Metroidvania games go this is natural. 

🌿 CONCLUSION: OATWOTW is an experience like no other any Metroidvania/platformer fan should have in their collection. Every step you take as Ori, feels like painting the world and leaving behind a mark nothing short of a masterpiece. It is sad to see it all end, but a well-polished story has no space for a continuation once all has been explained in great detail. The game will probably tug on your heart at times, but stay strong. This is one of those games that were created to keep you in the moment until the end, and a rewarding feeling for anyone expecting an emotional adventure that is not generic in any way.

[h1]The gist of it:[/h1]
Ori and the Will of the Wisps is everything The Blind Forest did but improved upon, an amazing platforming Metroidvania that should not be missed. 

👍 [u]The good parts:[/u]
+Combat has been extremely improved and it's great.
+Soundtrack is still emotional and impactful.
+Incredible boss fights and chase sequences.
+Great level design.

👎[u]The bad parts:[/u]
-Minor bugs and annoyances with the engine.
-The franchise needs better and deeper lore.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story starts exactly where the first game ended so if you haven't had the chance to finish The Blind Forest, it's mega important to do so. You play as Ori and this time around with the help of your flying friend you reach a new land where a similar incident has happened but much worse and you're tasked with restoring the land and restarting the cycle again. 

While there are some emotional scenes the story overall sadly feels way too similar to the first game. Hell, even the main villain is practically a copy of the last one which I felt was kinda cheap. It's not bad but I wish they did something else. 

Compared to the first one, this time around you'll also find a lot of unique characters that will offer obscure side quests for you to solve and I couldn't help but notice that they burrowed quite a lot from Hollow Knight, gameplay-wise as well but I'll detail that below. Side quests themselves are basic and are just a means for you to explore more of the levels. 

Overall it's technically an improvement over the first, however, I wanted more or something else with a bigger impact, emotional scenes aside. The locations and characters were practically screaming to have some lore attached to them. 

Story rating: 8.5/10

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Combat in The Blind Forest was a chore and it was boring as hell. Will of the Wisps comes with the opposite. As I mentioned above, the devs seem to have played and possibly enjoyed Hollow Knight so much that they've added similar skill mechanics to the game, such as having a huge number of talents or skills that you can equip and upgrade in your limited slots. These skills improve Ori's core stats and abilities. 

The main combat tree comes with several fighting and traversal abilities such as a sword or a huge mace or throwing stars at enemies and it feels really great to hit something this time around compared to the first game. The franchise at its core is still platforming and you'll still be jumping around the levels, finding secrets and trying to reach new places by going through tough but fair hazards. 

The best thing about the first game though was the chase sequences. They were fantastic and you can expect the same amazing sequences in Will of the Wisps as well but much better and some even longer. At some point, playing on hard, my hands started sweating at how tough and incredible at the same time the whole chase was. Curse you worm! 

But combat, platforming and chase sequences in a platformer Metroidvania could not be complete without boss fights and thankfully this time around they are great. Some easier than the other but I highly recommend playing on hard because at times it felt like I was fighting a boss in Dark Souls. Truly impressive that the devs spent the time to improve everything that was lacking in the first game. They deserve all the praise for making such satisfying gameplay. 

Gameplay rating: 9.5/10

[h1]Audio[/h1]
The moment you start the game and you hear that familiar music you know you'll be in for a treat with the soundtrack. Most songs are great and while the main ones are practically different versions/remixes of the same song, it brings life to the game and the scenes they play. The soundtrack adds so much to this game and I am sad that most game developers do not allocate time and resources to this particular asset. 

The voice acting and everything sound design related is as expected, good and nothing worth discussing over. Locations, skills, voices all sound good. 

Audio rating: 9/10

[h1]Graphics, performance and tech analysis[/h1]
Let's get the bad stuff out of the way first. The engine, it's not perfect, it hitches sometimes and for some users, including myself can end up being buggy. I was lucky to not encounter more than just a very few bugs but I've heard worse. 

Graphically speaking it looks the same as the first but with obvious improvements to the lighting and textures. Locations are pretty and varied, the characters you meet and fight are also very unique and well detailed. Boss fights look amazing and Ori's animations are well executed. 

Level design is also critical in a Metroidvania and just like the first game, everything falls into place perfectly. None of the zones feel separated from one another or randomly placed and I have to say that is very important to me. I've played many games in the same genre where you'd have an underwater level next to a desert place. None of that stuff here. Well done overall. 

Graphics, performance and tech analysis score:  9/10

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Ori and the Will of the Wisps launches the franchise to the top of the food chain and without a doubt it's one of the best Metroidvanias, no, games, ever made. Buy the game, it's incredible, but play the first one before it. 

[h1]Final score: 9/10[/h1]

Having just finished this masterpiece, I just had to come here and write a review, seeing as it is still relevant and many people have not played it yet.

Where to start..
Ori and the will of the wisps is the second Ori game, after Ori and the blind forest and therefore adds to the ending of the first game. It continues pretty much exactly where the first game left of, so it's adviced to play through the first game before picking up this one, or at least watching a playthrough of it, if you want to be fully invested into the story and characters.
Although, by the way they handle cutscenes, it might be possible to invest yourself into the characters, regardless of knowing the first game or not.

Which brings me to the first point of this review, the story. 
Man did I love the story, it feels like you're going through a beautifuly crafted fairytale and even more so than in the first game, your character is really in the midst of it all. The game has a beautiful way of telling it's story and for that alone it's worth to be played in my opinion.

Gameplay wise the game also felt great. Insanely smooth. The controlls are on point and reactive in any way imaginable. You get so many different abilities and options, that any place can be reached with a variety of different skills, which makes progression really fluent. Since the map is pretty open early on, you can chose where to go yourself and only backtrack to older locations once you found abilities to help you progress through the area. Pretty much every area teaches you a ability and as said before, each of them can be used in different ways. 

You can also equip a bunch of passive skills, something that is, unless I remember wrong, not something that you were able to do in the first Ori, but it feels nice to just have that extra edge to your character.

Visually.. I don't think I need to say much. The game is stunning. Beautiful scenery, beautiful characters, the music is amazing as well. The whole game is honestly just.. beautiful.

If I had to pinpoint something, that I didn't like about the game, it would be that sometimes it felt like there was a spike in difficulty. Never something that would be unbeatable, but I often found myself getting stuck in seemingly random locations for random reasons. Some of the plattforming can get pretty tricky later on, but after a few tries should be managed. I've often overlooked the solution to a puzzle as well, but that's probably on me.

In the end, Ori and the will of the wisps is an even better Ori and the blind forest. A strong sequel to an already strong prequel. The two go hand in hand with each other, just having this game improved in so many ways and strenghend with a lot of depht in all aspects.

It's absolutely worth to be played, I encourage everyone who is a fan of beautifuly crafted stories, plattformers or metroidvanias to play this game!

[i]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i] is an action-adventure platformer game and the sequel to the multi-award-winning [i]Ori and the Blind Forest.[/i] The game includes challenging puzzles, entertaining mechanics, and a deep story.

The storytelling is very emotional and engaging. There are many friendly non-player characters added to the game. The players can interact with those characters and listen to their stories. This feature makes the game world a livelier place.

Apart from the addition of boss fights, there are new challenges with high replay value in the game, such as combat shrines and spirit trials. The players can try their combat skills against waves of enemies by activating combat shrines or race against time by starting spirit trials.

The game includes abilities from the previous game as well as new ones. Besides the passive ones, the players are allowed to have only three abilities active at a time. However, they can customize their gameplay by switching between abilities throughout the game, even during combat.

The hand-painted artwork and great soundtracks are the most admirable aspects of the game. These aspects create a beautiful environment and a magical atmosphere within the game.

The game offers a decent challenge and a relaxing gaming experience at the same time. It is highly recommended for the players who enjoy cute, emotional and atmospheric games. Playing the first game before getting into this one would make the story more impressive.

Ori and the Will of the Wisps is the most beautiful game I ever played.

It's also a great metroidvania in terms of gameplay, combining the amazing movement tech and flow of the original Ori with some varied new combat abilities and the opportunities to use them. But what really makes it stand out is the sheer artistry that went into crafting its audio-visual presentation. With most games of non-trivial complexity, there are times when you can see the limits of either technology or budget. In this game, everything from the start to the end felt like it was implemented exactly as envisioned. Bravo.

The gorgeous environments, puzzles and escape scenes in Blind Forest were great, but Will of the Wisps really adds some things that make the game feel bigger and improved overall. There's more to do, more to see, and a new cast of characters that make the world, beautiful though it was, feel much less lonely than its predecessor. NPCs throughout the game actually speak to Ori, some of which sell upgrades, and many more who have side quests to complete. There is one area of the world, a sort of safe zone/central hub where all of the friendly characters gather, that Ori can build up and improve on over time by utilizing side quests and materials you find throughout the game, and I really enjoyed that feature, too.

Combat plays a much larger role this time around. Rather than just fleeing gigantic foes and oncoming hazards (which there is still plenty of!) one of the biggest changes in Will of the Wisps is the addition of boss fights, which I found to be a welcome one. There's just something more satisfying about actually being able to face them instead of just scrambling your way to a narrow escape every time.

As with Blind Forest, the difficulty is on the higher end, even on easy mode. It's a also a tearjerker, arguably even more so this time around. I really loved this series. I think it will always hold a special place in my heart.

 [h1] Review [/h1] 

Ori and the Will of the Wisps is everything the predecessor was and just the right amount of "so much more". I will not make a review of the game from the ground up as I already wrote a bit about Ori and the Blind Forest way back, which I still think suffice. What is the most interesting aspect of this specific installation is to compare it to what came before, even though I usually do not promote comparison tactics, these two games are so clearly cut from the same cloth they might as well be base game and expansion. This said, Ori and the Will of the Wisps truly is an upgrade.

This doesn't mean Blind Forest is a bad game, not by a long shot, but the things that could be improved upon has been so in the sequel. Most notably is the combat, where the button mashing homing missiles have been swapped with a plethora of "weapons" and abilities that each feel unique and fresh, while sticking to the clean and easy Ori formula and visuals. The basic attack you start off the game with is the lightsaber-esque melee attack that both is satisfying to use and more respondent and skillful than previous basic attack (the homing missiles). This sets a base level which is expanded upon throughout the game. How it is expanded upon also differs from Blind Forest.

The spirit trees are still here, so your movement arsenal will be gradually expanded upon as the game goes along, yet your combat abilities and stat buffs belong to the multiple inhabitants of the forest. Instead of using level points to advance a single skill tree, Will of the Wisps has an in game currency that is spent in different stores for combat abilities, quirks and maps. Although worried of it being tiresome at first, I soon cherished the travels back to the unexpected sort of "hub world" the game present where you will meet new friends and expand and develop your small part of the universe.

The game feels more alive due to the multiple characters you meet, when the previous game although vibrant in color and flora felt a bit empty. This is also evident through side missions, which are hardly impactful nor that interesting, but adds that extra level of immersion that makes you fall in love with the world Moon Studios have created. When a cute Moki asks you to find a hat for him to wear, it will bring you a smile.

The boss levels feel even more inspiring and varied now, with a mix of combat and escape sequences, while 3 slot ability hotkeys have just the right amount of depth in skill and satisfactory combat flow. The game have time trials built into the world which are set up to a leaderboard which really tickles my fancy as a speedrunning parkour Mirror's Edge nerd. What more could be said about this gem that hasn't already been said? Soundtrack is gorgeous, sound effects exemplary, art stunning and the story which I will not reveal, surprisingly hard hitting.

[h1]We Must Never Forget The Day, When Ori Enters Our Life. [/h1]

Two years ago I stumbled upon Ori and The Blind Forest and I was a blast to playthrough. The incredible music, the beautiful artstyle, the challenging platforming, and most importantly the touching story grasped my heart. Two years later Ori and The Will of The Wisp releases and I refuse to miss this gem by another year or two. Two hours sinking in and I am already impressed how the sequel improves greatly upon the first one.

[h1]Things I Love About Ori and The Will of The Wisp:[/h1]

[b]1. New and Fresh Combat System[/b]
The most noticeable problem from the first game is the combat system. In the first game, Sein is our companion and weapon. The combat revolves around this little orb shooting light darts at the enemies while Ori just standing there [strike]menacingly[/strike]. Players only need to mash one button over and over again. It certainly is boring and lacks variety. The sequel, however, makes a great leap. The developers definitely listen to players' opinions and come up with many things to improve the experience. So far I unlock several weapons and I enjoy using each and every of them. Let's take the sword for example. Freshly unlocked and it already contains many movesets: four-hits combo, downward thrust, upper slash that lifts enemies aloft. Manipulating these movesets yield a wonderful and satisfying combat experience. What`s even better is that later on when you unlock other weapons, you can assign them up to three different slots and fully utilizing them to dominate your opponents. My favorite combo is two slashes from the sword for starter, lifting the enemy up afterward, shooting it with two quick arrows, and finishing it with a downward smash from the hammer. To further customize your playstyle, the game introduces Spirit Shards to make adjustment to our little spirit of light. Additional health, faster arrows shooting, dealing more damage and taking more damage, regenerating health, you name it.

[b]2. Vivid Characters And Side Quests[/b]
The first game only have a few characters and is enough to make the story enticing. The second one, on the other hand, introduces many characters to make the world feel alive and vibrant. Tokk, a traveling blue bird who offers advice and lore in various locations, Opher, a skillful monkey and your combatant master, Moki, cute and fluffy meerkats-like creature that you can help throughout Wellspring Glades, and Kwolok, a giant toad and a kind guardian that offers you direction. I love every and each of them and I look forward to meeting more in the future. They invigorate my adventure to a wonderful journey. Along with new characters come with side quests. This is a nice addition to exploration. In the first game there are many hidden objects throughout the whole map. They are rewarding if you take time to find them, but they lack true purpose besides the joy of discovery. Now with side quests implemented in the second game, revisiting and discovering areas has new meaning. I don`t about others but I love the experience of completing the quests while also finding hidden spirit shards, health and energy fragments along the way.

[b]3. Real Boss Fights[/b]
The first game does not have "actual" boss fights other than running the hell away from Kuro's merciless pursuits. The second game makes sure this issue addressed. With new combat system comes with real boss fight. So far I encounter two boss fight and I enjoy our interaction. Both of them have great visual details and flash indicators of their attacks. Howler opens up with a classic cat-and-mouse chase and finally the player resort 1 on 1 combat with the torch in hand. Due to lacking evasive manuvers at early stage, player needs to be patient and out-space Howler's wide claw and sharp teeth. Don't be greedy even if taking one hit only reduce half of a health orb. It will do you no good in the long run. The other one is a giant armored beetle. This encounter requires you utilize the Dash to its full potential. Dash behind when it jumps, attack it soft spot on the back, double jump and air dash when it emits a fire shockwave. For metroidvania veterans these two boss fight certainly aren`t hard, but for Ori as a metroidvania they are unquestionably making the game outstanding in the genre.

[b]4. Music[/b]
[h1]Gareth Coker and Aeralie Brighton nail it right once again.[/h1]
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=76qRF5-qvZM
One of many reasons I love about Ori and the Blind Forest is the background music. The soothing yet somehow sad tone accompanying with the soft yet powerful vocal really touches my heart deeply, especially the theme of the main menu. I can literally stay on that screen and keep on listening to it.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EhcOVZdqnVM
Now when it comes to the second one, the vibe is not as strong as the first one. However, it definitely fits the theme of the game. If the first game is about a dying forest, then the second game is about finding your friend a different lively world. Listening to the first piece of the music I hear the wind sweeping the forest, birds chirping and later a tender, serene vocal emerges, like a nymph residing in the forest, singing the song of this vibrant paradise. I can never get enough of this. In game the background music is brighter and more delightful than the first one, once again reinforcing the idea of a spirited land full of beautiful creatures. I particularly love the part where you progress through certain part of the game, you will hear the familiar tone played once in a while. A throwback to the first game and a reminder of Ori's similar origin to the ancient spirit once dwell in this world.

[h1]Things I Hate About Ori and The Will of The Wisp:[/h1]

Very occaionally, the audio during cutscene would crash all of sudden, but resume to normal immediately.

[b]My brain[/b]: was overwhelmed by this one; it's maybe even more of an Action RPG than I expected with all the NPCs vs. sidequests, combat, and there's a huge world to explore! As one of few who didn't like Bastion at all, there's definitely a bittersweet taste due to my preferences. However, having finished this game in Normal mode, and as an (inefficient) explorer/someone inspecting every 'nook and cranny', I managed to make the game rather underwhelming closer to the finish — compensating the intensity, but maybe a too relaxed experience while enjoying the view, and making enough screenshots = lack of balance/players too spoilt with abilities and such? I felt too invincible at a certain moment, and it was mostly the beautiful music, scenery and the emotive storytelling that prevailed for me in this sequel and kept me going! 

Where it was rather stressful for me in the beginning — not confident enough in a fight, because of the lack of affinity with battling in general — I think I found the borders of arrogance near the end 😇 As a result, an important message to potential players: even though you will face 'dead ends' if you start exploring as much as possible right from the start (like I did), if you want an easy experience in Normal mode, and it's in your nature to discover, go ahead! If you prefer to stay focused on your main path, aren't thát distracted by sidequests etc. (unlike me) in general, and want to have a more challenging/brave experience, you know what to do instead. Fun fact though: there are Leaderboards that don't seem to update after a finish anymore; I was @ 85% by then, but a few of my friends were @ 87%, and 1 even @ 98%, so 'OPri' for sure!

Furthermore, it's rare, but even after so many hours, I'm still not 100% confident while playing this game with a keyboard (and so many buttons) ... Xbox Game Studios, right? I had expected the following notice: [i]"A controller is strongly recommended to play Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/i]". Talked about this with a friend, who initially started with keyboard controls, but soon realized the controller was the way to go. As a fan of both Super Meat Boy, and SMB Forever, I was excited for the Spirit Trials (races), but I wish there were just a few buttons mapped ... The escape sequences on the other hand were a breeze, and reminded me of aforementioned auto-runner.

10/11.4 — overwhelming in a good and bad way, but I now only feel to play the original once more!
New to the series? You definitely don't want to skip the original (Definitive Edition), but if you're very much into Action RPGs, combat, tactics etc., maybe think twice, and who knows start with the sequel ...

I don't remember much of the first game, besides that I really liked it. I got to this one pretty late, but I enjoyed it as well. The biggest strength is the movement; it feels amazing flying around the map with multiple jumps, boosts off enemies and their projectiles. You need to unlock a few abilities, takes maybe 90-120 minutes before the game really opens up and becomes a lot more enjoyable IMO. Once it did I was all in, up until that point I was a bit bored. 

The combat is easily one of the weakest parts of the game. If you've played games like [i]Hollow Knight[/i] and [i]Blasphemous 2[/i] to name a few examples, you're gonna be pretty let down by this aspect of the game. I honestly enjoy the escape sequences from the original Ori more than any of the boss fights here which are all super easy. The combat is so strange because everything is easy, but at the same time, making the enemies more challenging wouldn't necessary make it better because the attacks you have kinda just suck and feel underwhelming. I also found it really annoying that you can only have 3 abilities equipped at once; most games like this would typically allow you to use all your abilities via different button inputs, or a better control scheme so that felt pretty bad.

Similar to the original, the game is beautiful, and the music is amazing. It's certainly a game that is more accessible to newer Metroidvania players, and will be more enjoyable if you haven't played some of these other titles that have incredible combat. Regardless, it's still a fun experience and offers music and visuals that are thoroughly enjoyable. Not my favorite, but a good game that I'd recommend.

[h1]Review of “Ori and the Will of the Wisps”, also known as “Who cuts the onions Part Two”[/h1]
(TLDR at the end... just read a bit, you lazy person!)
[i]Recommendation: If you haven’t played the first game, you should play that one first![/i]

In the sequel to “Ori and the Blind Forest”, Ori’s journey continues, facing new enemies, meeting new friends and allies. The story that Moon Studios is telling is heartwarming. If you played the first game you should know by now that by purchasing this game, you will have to go the extra mile and invest in some safety-tissues! Jokes asides (well it wasn’t really a joke)
After having played through the game three times, Ori and The Will of the Wisps is one of my personal favorite games. Ori’s second adventure takes the foundation of what made the first game so special and revolutionizes the formular and expands in scale, size, and quality in all aspects.

First of all, there is the new fighting system. Fighting in “The Blind Forest” was fun, but the aspect that got overhauled the most for this game. Ori can now choose between different weapons that handle fundamentally different: From a Sword, bow and spear to a hammer. Each one requires a different playstyle during combat and has its advantages and disadvantages against the huge enemy variety. Passive skills in form of shards, can be found and many new abilities get unlocked the further you get into the game. The controls are snappy, Ori always does what you expect him to do and when you die, you never feel like it is the games’ fault. Whatever you do, the input translated into the character-movement perfectly.

In Will of the Wisps, Ori’s story continues right where the previous game ended. Without spoiling anything, the themes of friendship, family and love play a big role. On the way Ori meets many new friends in different areas, each featuring a unique biome that also adds new gameplay twists and puzzle elements to the gameplay-mix.  The general flow of the game is well executed, the pacing and difficulty scaling always felt well balanced…and yes: the escape sequences also make a comeback! bossfights and these well-known Escape sequences test your acquired skillset while never being unfair. You will die a lot, but overcoming each challenge feels super satisfying! (No need for tissues here!...[spoiler]except you are a pervert[/spoiler])
The platforming feels as great as ever. The traversal through the different areas always feels satisfying and the level design itself features lots of variety and different gameplay-mechanics.

All of that is supported by exceptional graphics powered by Moonity (MoonStudios modified Unity engine, check out the DigitalFoundry Interview to see how it works in action!). The superb lighting system, the beautifully handcrafted art assets, the physically based “squash and stretch” animations and lots of tiny details make each rendered look like a painting!
When we talk about Ori, we cannot forget to talk about the exceptional soundtrack. Gareth Coker elevates Ori’s emotional journey with a fitting heartwarming, intense soundtrack for each part of the game. Ori’s theme from the original game gets some fresh takes, getting woven together with new themes. Each new character and environment get treated musically with a thematic approach. The soundtrack strikes the right amount of “Damn bitches, I’m back!”-nostalgia feeling and “that new piece sounds quite sick!” that you would want for a sequel! …Seriously, the game is worth it for the music alone already!

[h1][b]TLDR / Summary[/b]

All in all, “Ori and the Will of the Wisps” has fun and challenging gameplay, with a beautiful visuals and music that result in atmosphere. No matter if you have played any platforming game before or not, you should give the Ori games a try!  The emotional story results in a heartwarming and memorable journey that you shouldn’t miss! It is one of those games I can play over and over again, with my mighty tissue box next to me, escaping the world for a while.[h1]

Ori and the Will of the Wisps is an action platformer and the sequel to Ori and the Blind Forest.

Having played the first game a lot, and most of it quite recently, I naturally couldn’t wait for the sequel. I was a bit worried that it might be too different, yet not different enough to feel good - but nothing of that mattered anymore the instant I started playing: It felt great!

Ori and the Will of the Wisps has lost nothing of what made the first game so good, meaning the platforming and the movement mechanics, basically. At the core it’s still the same, with some additions, mostly more complex combat than in the first game, and a much bigger map with more content. There’s more variety in a lot of things, and I want to mention the soundtrack specifically for that aspect: The soundtrack in the first game was great too, but it consisted of variations of the same theme for the most part. It feels much more diverse here. 

The gameplay is fun, as well as as the overall world, the boss fights, escape sequences (although there was one I had quite some trouble with and I ended up kind of hating it, as the most important mechanic didn’t feel very precise. I’m not sure how much of that is my fault, but the other escapes felt rather easy, so it was weird). 
The NPCs are well-designed, there are side quests and other activities you can do, apart from collecting stuff throughout the map - and completing the main story, of course.

To me it feels like most of the additions and changes compared to the first game really were aspects that people didn’t like so much or would have wished for in the original Ori, so that’s a plus, too. Many of those changes feel similar to Hollow Knight, but to the right extent: It definitely is still an Ori game, but it might appeal a bit more to fans of Hollow Knight who didn’t like Blind Forest so much. 

Many have said it before, and I was no exception: I had some minor bugs and glitches, as well as one game crash. I was lucky, it didn’t happen very often, and there was nothing gamebreaking for me. Also, all problems were solved after I restarted the game, but still a bit annoying. Things are probably going to be fixed soon, so it might be a good idea to wait for a few more days if you’re not too eager to play right away.

Not taking this too much into account for the overall experience, I do recommend the game - very much. Compared to Blind Forest I wouldn’t necessarily say it’s better, it’s a bit different and it offers more (personally, I think I prefer the first one as I think the level design is better in Blind Forest). But in comparison or on its own, doesn’t matter, because I do think it’s a great game!

[h2]Ori and the Will of the Wisps[/h2]
[i]A most worthy successor.[/i]

[h3]Preclaimer[/h3]
- This is the story related successor to [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/0256667/recommended/387290/]Ori and the Blind Forest[/url], which I will be heavily referencing throughout this review.

[hr]
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2669165974[/url]
[hr]
[h3]Gameplay & Quality[/h3]
Ori and the Will of the Wisps is, just like its predecessor, a 2D Platformer with Metroidvania-style progression. Platforming puzzles, secrets and this time enhanced combat are all over the place. Just like before the game is focussing on creating a breathtaking atmosphere all throughout the story, though this time the actual storytelling part has been notably extended.

The gameplay generally stayed the same as before - you are controlling our little spirit of light, Ori, through the vast and beautifully designed open world while fighting enemies, gaining and leveling new abilities and so unlocking new areas to go to. But aside from this core concept, almost everything else changed - for the better, I'd say.

The open world now has an actual "open" world feeling to it. Instead of the linear story to follow we rather get a quest system with main story and optional side quests to follow as we find them. At some points the main story just tells you to go to certain areas, but in which order is up to you - of course for some you still need certain abilities to get there.

Alongside the side quests comes a whole bunch of NPCs to meet throughout the world, turning the subtle background narration into actual storytelling at the cost of lots and lots of dialogue to read, because everyone is still talking in an unintelligible language.

The exp and leveling system has been replaced by something that can be seen on other modern titles of this genre, e.g. Hollow Knight, as we just collect spirit light as some sort of currency. With this currency we can buy and upgrade new skills, spirit shards - which are equipable passive abilities, limited by the amount of slots you have - and even build, with resources found in the world, our own village.

Speaking of abilities, they have been reworked too. Instead of one set of fixed abilities we get three slots to equip three different ones at a time, changable anytime. The Soul Link has been replaced by a normal heal because this game now features auto-saving.

With all of these new abilities, combat changed a fair bit too. Instead of that one spammable auto aim ranged attack we focus on melee fighting now, with some mostly manual ranged attacks later on. Of course you can get by just fine with only the default attack, though the new skills have their fair share of uses and are fun to use. Most utilized are the bow and the throwable light orb known from the previous game, which you will need a lot to solve certain puzzles.
And the most drastic change: We now have actual boss fights!

New mechanics like climbing on walls and even the roof where blue grass grows, moving map elements and digging through sand and snow walls also make an appearance.

And finally, teleporting to warp stones is now possible from anywhere and maps are bought from an NPC you can find in every area.


Talking about performance and bugs for a moment, there are two things I noticed.
First off, the game has two FPS settings. One is for the "target FPS", meaning that the game utilizes automatic resolution and quality downscaling to reach this number when your PC is unable to keep up. This is set to 60 by default. The other is the hard enforced FPS limit. This is set to unlimited by default, using all available resources on your PC to reach unnecessary FPS ranges, creating audio and visual errors in at least one crowded area. Turning that down is highly recommended.

Second, the game seems to be a bit wonky with granting collector achievements. For me it only granted those achievements after I went to the main menu and loaded the save file again after completing it.

Otherwise the game runs smooth as usual, and while [b]the controls are different from before[/b] on the fixed keys, taking some getting used to, it's comfortably playable with a controller.

[hr]
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2669165763[/url]
[hr]
[h3]Content & Runtime[/h3]
What can you expect from this game?
An epic and emotional sequel and conclusion to the story told in Ori and the Blind Forest.

Following the events of the predecessor, our new journey begins where we left off - after the forest of Nibel was saved and Kuro's final possession, the last remaining egg, hatched. Ori and the newborn Ku, who sadly suffers from a deformed wing, live a happy life as a family, until with the passing of time Ku's yearning for the sky grows ever stronger.

Finding a makeshift solution to fix her broken wing and enabling her to finally fly, Ori and Ku set out on a journey. Though this happy day and their newfound freedom soon turn dark, as they get into another heavy storm and get separated in a faraway land.

Will Ori be able to find Ku and get them safely back home before anything happens? And what is the story of this dark and desolate forest devoid of light?


Once again we get a beautiful, emotional story told along the journey of the player, through interactive cutscenes, lots of dialogue with NPCs and whatever remnants of the past this new world has to show. Of course the on-spot and meaningful soundtrack can't be missed.

Completing this journey fully took me [b]short of 15h[/b], 100%ing the game. Compared to the predecessor we only get the default three difficulties to choose from, taking away notable replayability, but instead we get a few racing minigames with ingame leaderboards dedicated people can compete in.

Sadly we don't have a gallery for all the cutscenes or addional media anymore. I'd have loved to re-view all those important story moments.

[hr]
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2669165797[/url]
[hr]
[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
Is this game worth it?
Yep. Ori and the Will of the Wisps is a beautiful and worthy standalone game, even more so if you played and enjoyed the predecessor. Of course you should have played the predecessor before taking on this one, and the huge price increase compared to the little increase in playtime might sound bad, so I once again recommend buying the bundle with a little discount.
Because the next sale is always around the corner!
